{"id":"persona-3tly.4","title":"Record the limits of the presence model in the spec","description":"Three properties cannot be engineered away and should be written down rather than rediscovered. SPEC-HIA describes presence levels as though they are measurements; these are the boundaries of what any implementation can mean by them.

1. 'Right now' is a category error. Presence is continuous; a bearer token is discrete. Signing one asserts a duration for an instant that was observed. Shortening the TTL approaches truth asymptotically and reaching zero means a touch per request, which nobody will use. A credential can say when presence was observed; it cannot say presence persists.

2. 'In front of the machine' is not what any signal measures. SSH from another continent, RDP, a key on a USB extension in the next room, and 'screen unlocked' meaning unlocked at some past moment are all indistinguishable from a human at the keyboard. Every attestor measures proximity to an authenticator, not proximity to a machine.

3. Coercion is undetectable. The strongest available presence signal is fully satisfiable under duress. No presence model distinguishes a willing human from a compelled one, and none should claim to.

Suggested wording for what the daemon can defensibly assert, which is materially weaker than the current docs: 'at time T, an authenticator enrolled to this identity produced a signature requiring physical interaction, and personad verified it.'

This matters beyond honesty. The presence model is the part of HIA that SPIFFE does not already cover and the part a standards body would scrutinise, so its limits should be stated by the spec rather than found by a reviewer.","notes":"Reframing from Mark: stating the gap is not a confession, it is an invitation. A limit named precisely enough becomes a work item for standards bodies, vendors and government programmes rather than an apology. Write this section so it is FILLABLE — name what a filler would have to provide, not merely what persona cannot do.

His prediction for what fills it, and it is convincing: 'the CAC card is still plugged in', most of the time. That answer is already deployed at scale under HSPD-12, and it beats a FIDO2 tap on the axis that matters here, because card removal is an event rather than an expiry guess. It also works for a non-technical reason worth recording in the spec: the CAC is simultaneously the building badge and the photo ID, so a physical and social constraint keeps it with the human. No protocol supplies that.

So the section should distinguish limits that are genuinely unfillable (coercion) from limits that are unfilled BY THIS DAEMON and invite an answer (continuity of presence, binding to intent). {"description":"Three properties cannot be engineered away and should be written down rather than rediscovered. SPEC-HIRE describes presence levels as though they are measurements; these are the boundaries of what any implementation can mean by them.

1. 'Right now' is a category error. Presence is continuous; a bearer token is discrete. Signing one asserts a duration for an instant that was observed. Shortening the TTL approaches truth asymptotically and reaching zero means a touch per request, which nobody will use. A credential can say when presence was observed; it cannot say presence persists.

2. 'In front of the machine' is not what any signal measures. SSH from another continent, RDP, a key on a USB extension in the next room, and 'screen unlocked' meaning unlocked at some past moment are all indistinguishable from a human at the keyboard. Every attestor measures proximity to an authenticator, not proximity to a machine.

3. Coercion is undetectable. The strongest available presence signal is fully satisfiable under duress. No presence model distinguishes a willing human from a compelled one, and none should claim to.

Suggested wording for what the daemon can defensibly assert, which is materially weaker than the current docs: 'at time T, an authenticator enrolled to this identity produced a signature requiring physical interaction, and hired verified it.'

This matters beyond honesty. The presence model is the part of HIA that SPIFFE does not already cover and the part a standards body would scrutinise, so its limits should be stated by the spec rather than found by a reviewer."}
